title: Article 1 — Name and territory of the Union

content.overview: Article 1 establishes that India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States; identifies the States and Union territories by reference to the First Schedule; and defines the territory of India as comprising the territories of the States, the Union territories in the First Schedule, and such other territories as may be acquired.
content.glance: India, that is Bharat = Union of States. Territory = States + UTs (First Schedule) + acquired territories. No right of secession.
content.study:
Article 1 is the opening structural provision of Part I (The Union and its Territory).

Text:
(1) India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States.
(2) The States and the territories thereof shall be as specified in the First Schedule.
(3) The territory of India shall comprise— (a) the territories of the States; (b) the Union territories specified in the First Schedule; and (c) such other territories as may be acquired.

‘Union of States’ (not a compact federation): the Constituent Assembly deliberately chose ‘Union’ to emphasise that the Indian polity is not a voluntary association of States with a right to secede. States are creatures of the Constitution; their existence, names, boundaries and territories are alterable under Articles 2–4.

First Schedule: authoritative list of States and Union territories and their territories. Changes to the Schedule are effected by laws under Articles 2 and 3 (see Article 4).

Acquired territories: clause (3)(c) permits inclusion of territories acquired by India (cession, conquest, or other modes recognised in international law), which then form part of the territory of India.

Relationship with Articles 2–4: Article 1 states the structure; Articles 2 and 3 confer power on Parliament to admit, establish, form and reorganise States; Article 4 allows such laws to amend the First and Fourth Schedules and provides that they are not amendments under Article 368.

sections.heading: Constitutional text
sections.body:
(1) India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States.
(2) The States and the territories thereof shall be as specified in the First Schedule.
(3) The territory of India shall comprise—
(a) the territories of the States;
(b) the Union territories specified in the First Schedule; and
(c) such other territories as may be acquired.

sections.heading: Union of States — structural meaning
sections.body: The expression ‘Union of States’ signals an indestructible Union with destructible States: the Union is permanent; individual States may be reorganised, renamed, merged or altered by Parliament under Articles 2–4. There is no constitutional right of secession. This distinguishes the Indian model from classical federal compacts in which constituent units retain a residual right to leave.

sections.heading: First Schedule and territory
sections.body: Clause (2) incorporates the First Schedule by reference. Clause (3) defines the territory of India exhaustively as States + Union territories in the First Schedule + acquired territories. Cession of territory (e.g. boundary adjustments with a foreign State) has been held to require constitutional authority; mere executive action is insufficient where sovereignty is transferred.

sections.heading: Exam and drafting checkpoints
sections.body:
1. State the full text of clauses (1)–(3).
2. Explain ‘Union of States’ vs federation with secession rights.
3. Link First Schedule changes to Articles 2–4 (and Article 4’s non-368 character).
4. Distinguish States from Union territories.
5. For cession/acquisition problems, discuss clause (3)(c) and the need for constitutional/legislative authority.

examples.title: Illustration — Reorganisation does not destroy the Union
examples.body: Parliament forms a new State by dividing an existing State under Article 3. Article 1 continues to describe India as a Union of States; only the First Schedule entries change (via the Article 3/4 law). The Union itself is unaffected.

examples.title: Illustration — Acquired territory
examples.body: Territory lawfully acquired by India becomes part of the territory of India under Article 1(3)(c). Its administration and eventual placement in the First Schedule (as State or UT) are governed by subsequent parliamentary law under Articles 2–4 and ordinary legislation.

hypotheticals.question: Can a State legislature pass a resolution declaring secession from the Union?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Article 1 constitutes India as a Union of States with no right of secession. States are not parties to a dissoluble compact. Any such resolution is unconstitutional. Parliament’s power to reorganise States under Articles 2–4 does not imply a reciprocal State power to leave the Union.

distinctions.title: Union of States vs classical federation

rows.right: May reserve residual exit rights to units

rows.left: Parliament may form/alter States under Arts 2–4
rows.right: Often requires unit consent or special procedure

rows.left: Constitution is supreme; States are its creatures

misconceptions.trap: India is a federation of States that can secede.
misconceptions.correction: Article 1 establishes a Union of States. There is no right of secession. States may be reorganised by Parliament under Articles 2–4.

misconceptions.trap: The First Schedule cannot be changed without a formal Article 368 amendment.
misconceptions.correction: Article 4 provides that laws under Articles 2 and 3 may amend the First and Fourth Schedules and that such laws are not amendments of the Constitution for the purposes of Article 368.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Explain Article 1 of the Constitution of India.
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Article 1 provides: (1) India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States; (2) the States and their territories shall be as specified in the First Schedule; (3) the territory of India comprises the territories of the States, the Union territories in the First Schedule, and such other territories as may be acquired. The phrase ‘Union of States’ emphasises an indestructible Union; States have no right to secede and may be reorganised by Parliament under Articles 2–4. The First Schedule is the authoritative list of units; changes to it are effected by laws under Articles 2–4, which Article 4 declares are not amendments under Article 368.

cases.name: In re Berubari Union and Exchange of Enclaves
cases.holding: Cession of Indian territory to a foreign State requires constitutional authority; the executive cannot cede territory by pure executive action. Implementation may require a constitutional amendment where the Constitution so demands.

examTips: Explain ‘Union of States’ and absence of secession right.
Link First Schedule changes to Article 4 (not Article 368).
